meta.title: In defense of not understanding your codebase
meta.author: siddhartha_golu

comments.author: typesanitizer
comments.text:
Unfortunately the original article has the clickbait title. The content of the article is closer to "you need to be able to make progress with partial understanding in large codebases."

The other aspect is, the theory building view is not actually in tension with the points in the article once you recognize that a theory can have both breadth and depth. Breadth is about what parts for the system do you sufficiently understand to be able to answer questions, make changes deftly etc. Depth is about how complex questions can you answer about a particular part of the system & how complex changes can you make while preserving integrity.

When you're rewriting some code module-by-module, where maybe you have a transition period, you're essentially building a narrow but deep theory of that module, and working based off of that. For small functions, adding an extra parameter or a return value works fine. But when you get to a larger scale, it starts to make sense to instead start from a "clean slate" (for that particular module!) and wire up other things to call the new thing, because trying to incrementally improve correctness of something that is fundamentally buggy doesn't work (this also often applies to properties like performance).

Now, one could debate what Naur actually meant by:


In preference to program revival, the Theory Building View suggests, the existing program text should be discarded, and the new-formed programmer team should be given the opportunity to solve the given problem afresh.


Does he literally mean the the old code should be deleted first before starting the rewrite? Or does he merely mean that the code should be discarded without any specific prescription for when (e.g. after the new program has been established to be an adequate replacement)?

The other thing is, the "given problem" is not actually given. Naur is assuming that you still have the original problem definition, but in practice, you don't for many large codebases. The closest thing to this is usually the test suite -- and so yeah, you can replace things while trying to keep the test suite passing.

Another thing to keep in mind is that, at the time, there was no such things as "continuous delivery." Today, you have services that are always running, and you have to hold a pager, answer questions, resolve immediate bugs etc. This also affects the calculus for rewrites.

comments.author: andyc
comments.text:
There are some things about this push back that are nicely worded ...

But I do feel it's mostly obvious -- partial understanding is the only state in a sufficiently big system, but institutions should always strive for MORE understanding.


On "you are being paid to do a job" - big software frequently fails to satisfy its users or meet its business goals.  Windows and OS X are arguably rotting from accumulated complexity.

I am sure if that management could wave a wand and remove that complexity, they would.  But it's just an unsolved problem in software engineering.  I don't think management WANTS people to ship bad code -- it's just the tradeoff they've accepted, given the status quo.

In other words, you could argue that "having a monopoly is good enough, so we can ship shitty, buggy software", but that is a pretty nihilistic take

And certainly many/most software shops don't have monopolies or users held hostage, and quality does matter in that case

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
Another aspect of modern development that differs from 1985 is that even if you become an expert in a 300,000 line codebase, you might be working on a different 300,000 line codebase next week. Experienced industry programmers become used to the idea that they might get parachuted into uncharted territory at a moment's notice and they have to rely on some combination of shared idioms (c.f. Google C++ Style Guide), mechanized tooling (compiler errors if you use an API wrong), and gut instinct about how large-scale programs "should" be structured.

I've seen discussion on this site and elsewhere about things like the LLM-driven Bun rewrite, roughly "now that no human being has a full understanding of how the codebase works how will they ever be able to continue developing it?", which is sort of like asking how it's possible to understand a novel without being the author. It's code. You can read it. If you don't understand what some function is doing you can carve it up into chunks, try writing some tests for it, write its control flow out on paper, whatever.

And since you'll be switching between projects with some regularity there's no point in maintaining your understanding of previous codebases. At some point it all just kinda blurs together. Your company acquired a startup and they need help getting their Scala code speaking some custom Thrift-based RPC protocol to talk to your JSON-based Ruby service that's being actively rewritten in Go? OK, whatever, an hour googling "Scala syntax reference" and "Thrift wire encoding" will get you started. You don't have to become an expert, there'd be no point, in a month you'll be debugging why an OCaml-based type checker for JavaScript crashes in a Go implementation of the Linux kernel. It's all just code.

comments.author: mxey
comments.text:
I've seen discussion on this site and elsewhere about things like the LLM-driven Bun rewrite, roughly "now that no human being has a full understanding of how the codebase works how will they ever be able to continue developing it?", which is sort of like asking how it's possible to understand a novel without being the author. It's code. You can read it. If you don't understand what some function is doing you can carve it up into chunks, try writing some tests for it, write its control flow out on paper, whatever.


To me it's not about whether anybody has the full code base in their head, but rather if the code is even written in a way that a human can reasonably work on it anymore, which is why readability is a big part of code review. Thousands of AI generated commits have obviously not been reviewed by anybody.


And since you'll be switching between projects with some regularity there's no point in maintaining your understanding of previous codebases.


This feels like saying specialised expertise has no value because it's not universally useful.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
[...] readability is a big part of code review. Thousands of AI generated commits have obviously not been reviewed by anybody.


I've worked at places that did or did not do code reviews, and the overall structure of the code (how the data flows between functions, relationship between modules, use of privacy/visibility to enforce invariants) IMO has a much stronger influence on long-term maintenance. The notation doesn't matter much until you get into the really obscure stuff, and LLMs seem to do fairly well -- the worst part of LLM-generated code is that the comments are all nonsense, which can be solved by stripping them out.


This feels like saying specialised expertise has no value because it's not universally useful.


It's helpful to distinguish between expertise and trivia. Learning how a parser works is expertise; so is being able to write a parser for a complex binary format without introducing security vulnerabilities. But knowing which specific file the build_huffman_tables() function lives in and the order of its parameters are trivia.

comments.author: mcherm
comments.text:
The approach described in the article is closely related to one's ability to reason locally about a piece of code.

The ability to understand one portion of a larger codebase without understanding the things around it (to "reason locally") is a key concept computer science has been pursuing from the beginning.

The primary advantage of "Structured Programming" (1968; Djikstra, among others) was the ability to reason locally. The recommendation to avoid global variables is largely in order to be able to reason locally. A major strength of functional programming (1977, Backus, among others) is the elimination of side effects which permits one to reason locally. One tenent of Object Oriented programming (1972 Kay, among others) was linking data structures with the code that operates on them, providing a different means for reasoning locally.

The true power of these fundamental concepts is that with them it is possible (although never desirable) to reason about or work on a small piece of a code base without understanding the entirety of it.

comments.author: 0x2ba22e11
comments.text: Just a nitpick but I'd call it software engineering rather than computer science, but yeah local reasoning is IMO the most useful thing in software engineering.

comments.author: jo3_l
comments.text:
I am not sure whether you are aware, but lobste.rs uses the vibecoding tag to broadly describe all content related to LLM usage, a practice I disagree with but is nonetheless the norm. In this case, the central question that the article deals with is one intimately related to LLM-assisted coding.

That said, I agree with you that the vibecoding tag should not be the only tag. The post does not explicitly mention LLMs until the very end, and the point it makes is interesting and worth discussion even in a pre-LLM era. This is enough of an argument to justify restoring the practices tag, IMO, which I have done and suggest others to do the same.

comments.author: mcherm
comments.text:
The point made in the article is meaningful to any programmer, especially one who wants to understand how to grapple with giant codebases, and how that is different from smaller projects.

The point is also relevant in a world where the use of LLMs might impede people's full understanding of the codebase.

If the tag means "this might be relevant to people interested in vibecoding", then it clearly applies. If the tag means " this is irrelevant except to people interested in vibecoding", then it doesn't apply. All other tags are used in the first sense, but a notable percentage of the Lobsters userbase uses this tag in the second sense. I guess those folks will just have to miss out.

comments.author: coxley
comments.text:
In sufficiently large codebases, everyone operates with an incorrect theory of the program.


While true, having a subset of people strive to close the gap is an important goal. Even if it's never complete, it'll get out of control if you do nothing, because large codebases continually grow. The gap of assumed <=> correct theory widens.

The most common fall out I see is: team attempts X, it doesn't work as expected, and they dismiss X as not suitable. When in reality, the system wasn't set up in a way for X to even make sense yet.


"We tried Misra-Gries to identify top talkers, but it was too inaccurate": it was used to track asymmetrically weighted events.

"We tried load shedding, but it rejected too much traffic": most load was from retry storms, which needed fixed first.


When the nuances are abstracted, it's too easy to run "false experiments" like that and move on to complicating the system instead.
